title: Availability Zones
primary_service: AWS account, infrastructure and billing setup
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of availability zones and its relationship to AWS Global Infrastructure and Account Setup.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to availability zones.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn availability zones in the context of AWS Global Infrastructure and Account Setup. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Availability Zones matters because it is one part of aws account, infrastructure and billing setup. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: AWS global infrastructure
content_blocks.alt_text: A simplified hierarchy relates Regions, Availability Zones, and workloads while highlighting account and data-residency decisions.
content_blocks.caption: A Region is a geographic area; Availability Zones are separate fault-isolation locations within it.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Availability Zones belongs to AWS Global Infrastructure and Account Setup. AWS resource placement, account boundaries, access safety, billing visibility and cleanup are one joined workflow. Start with a controlled, approved learning environment.

The PDF lists these subtopics: What an Availability Zone is; Using multiple Availability Zones; Availability Zones and fault isolation. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For availability zones, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Availability Zones”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Availability Zones with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.
